dryRun.title: Prefix sums of [2, 4, 1, 3], then the sum of indexes 1..2
dryRun.note: The prefix array has one extra slot at the front (a 0). Then any range sum is one subtraction: prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].

think.q:
const nums = [2, 4, 1, 3]
const p = [0]
for (const x of nums) p.push(p[p.length - 1] + x)
console.log(p.join(","), p[3] - p[1])
why: p[k] is the sum of the first k items. The array is 5 long because of the extra leading 0.
p[3] - p[1] is 7 - 2 = 5, which is nums[1] + nums[2] = 4 + 1.
think.exec:
const nums = [2, 4, 1, 3]
const p = [0]
for (const x of nums) p.push(p[p.length - 1] + x)
console.log(p.join(","), p[3] - p[1])

think.q: With p[0] = 0 and p[k] = sum of the first k items, what is the sum of nums[l..r] (both ends included)?
why: p[r + 1] holds everything up to and including index r. Subtracting p[l] removes everything before l.
The extra leading 0 is what makes l = 0 work without a special case.

think.q: You have n numbers and q range-sum questions. What is the total time with a prefix array?
why: Building the prefix array is O(n), and each question is one subtraction, O(1). Total O(n + q).
Summing each range again by hand costs O(n) per question, so O(n * q).

think.q:
const nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 3
const seen = new Map([[0, 1]])
let sum = 0, count = 0
for (const x of nums) {
  sum += x
  count += seen.get(sum - k) || 0
  seen.set(sum, (seen.get(sum) || 0) + 1)
}
console.log(count)
why: The subarrays that add up to 3 are [1, 2] and [3], so the answer is 2.
A subarray ends here with sum k exactly when an earlier prefix equals sum - k. The map counts those earlier prefixes.

think.q: In the "subarray sum equals k" code, the map starts as { 0: 1 }. Why?
opts: To avoid an empty map error
So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
Because the first number is always 0
why: A subarray from index 0 has prefix = sum and nothing before it. That is the same as "an earlier prefix of 0", so we pretend one exists.
Without the seed, [1, 2] with k = 3 would be missed.

try.task: Write rangeSums(nums, queries). Each query is [l, r] (both included). Return the array of range sums. It must run in O(n + q).
try.hint: Build p with a leading 0. Then each answer is p[r + 1] - p[l].

checks.verify: const n = 100000; const nums = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i % 7); const qs = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => [i % 50, n - 1 - (i % 50)]); const t0 = Date.now(); const out = rangeSums(nums, qs); assert(out.length === n && Date.now() - t0 < 300, "too slow, are you re-adding every range?")

takeaway.key: Build prefix sums once (with a leading 0), then every range sum is p[r + 1] - p[l]. With a map of earlier prefixes it also counts subarrays with a given sum.
mistakes: Off-by-one: using p[r] when r is inclusive.
Forgetting to seed the map with { 0: 1 }.
Using a sliding window when numbers can be negative (it needs prefix sums).

dryRun.title: Smallest ship capacity to carry [3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 4] in at most 3 days
dryRun.note: The answer is not in an array. It is a number between max item (4) and sum of all (16). For each guess we count days, which gives a yes or no, and that yes/no flips only once.

think.q:
const w = [3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 4]
const days = (cap) => {
  let d = 1, cur = 0
  for (const x of w) {
    if (cur + x > cap) { d++; cur = 0 }
    cur += x
  }
  return d
}
console.log(days(10), days(7), days(5))
why: Capacity 10: [3,2,2], then [4,1,4] = 2 days. Capacity 7: [3,2,2], [4,1], [4] = 3 days. Capacity 5 needs 4 days.
A bigger capacity never needs more days. This one-way behaviour is what makes binary search legal.

think.q: For "smallest capacity to ship all packages in D days", what is the smallest sensible lower bound for the search?
why: A ship smaller than the heaviest package could never carry it. So the answer is at least max(weights).
The upper bound is the sum: one ship carrying everything in one day.

think.q: You want the largest x such that ok(x) is true, and ok goes T T T F F. When ok(mid) is true, what is the safe move?
opts: lo = mid, with the upper middle: mid = lo + ceil((hi - lo) / 2)
why: mid works, but something bigger might too. So keep it: lo = mid.
With the normal lower middle, lo = mid can loop forever when hi = lo + 1. Using the upper middle fixes that.

think.q: Each guess costs one O(n) pass. The answer range has size S. What is the total time?
why: Binary search tries about log₂(S) guesses, and each one scans the n items.
Trying every capacity one by one would be O(n * S).

think.q: Which wording usually points to "binary search on the answer"?
opts: "Return all pairs that sum to k"
"Minimize the largest...", "maximize the smallest...", "find the minimum speed such that..."
why: These ask for the best value of something, and a bigger or smaller value only ever makes it easier or harder.
If you can test one guess quickly and the yes/no flips only once, you can search for the boundary.

try.task: Write minCapacity(weights, days). Packages must be shipped in the given order, each day a ship carries a run of packages with total weight at most the capacity. Return the smallest capacity that ships everything within days days.
try.hint: Search lo = max(weights), hi = sum(weights). For each mid, count the days greedily. If days <= limit, hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1.

checks.t: as many days as packages means the heaviest

takeaway.key: When a guess can be tested in O(n) and the answer flips from "no" to "yes" only once, binary search the answer: O(n log S). Pick bounds that surely contain it.
mistakes: Wrong bounds (a lower bound that is too small, or an upper bound that cannot work).
Using lo = mid with the lower middle and looping forever.
Testing a guess with a check that is not monotonic.
Mixing up "minimize" (first true) and "maximize" (last true) updates.

dryRun.title: Kadane's on [2, -5, 3, 4, -1]
rows: keep going, but the sum is negative now
dryRun.note: cur is the best sum of a subarray that ends here. If the sum before is negative, it only hurts, so we restart. The answer is the best cur seen: 7 (the subarray [3, 4]).

think.q:
let cur = 0, best = -Infinity
for (const x of [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) {
  cur = Math.max(x, cur + x)
  best = Math.max(best, cur)
}
console.log(best)
why: The best subarray is [4, -1, 2, 1] with sum 6.
At each item there are only two choices: extend the old subarray, or start a new one at this item.

think.q:
let cur = 0, best = 0
for (const x of [-3, -1, -2]) {
  cur = Math.max(x, cur + x)
  best = Math.max(best, cur)
}
console.log(best)

The correct answer is -1 (the best non-empty subarray). What does this print?
why: Starting best = 0 means "an empty subarray with sum 0" always wins. The code returns 0, which is wrong when every number is negative.
Start with best = -Infinity (or nums[0]).

think.q: At index i, what does cur hold?
opts: The sum of the whole array so far
The best subarray sum anywhere in the array
The best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at i
why: It must end at i, so the next item can extend it. best is the separate variable that remembers the maximum over all i.
Mixing the two up is the most common bug.

think.q: When should the running subarray be dropped and a new one started at x?
opts: When the running sum before x is negative (it can only make things worse)
When x is the maximum so far
why: A negative running sum added to anything makes it smaller, so starting fresh at x is better. That is exactly max(x, cur + x).
A negative x alone is fine to include if the sum before it is big.

think.q: What are the time and extra space of Kadane's algorithm?
why: One pass and two numbers: cur and best. Trying every subarray would be O(n²) or O(n³).
It is a tiny dynamic programming idea with the table shrunk to one value.

try.task: Write maxSubarray(nums). Return the largest sum of a non-empty run of neighbouring items.
try.hint: Keep cur (best sum ending here) and best. For each x: cur = Math.max(x, cur + x), then best = Math.max(best, cur). Start best at the first item, not 0.

checks.verify: const big = Array.from({ length: 200000 }, (_, i) => (i % 3 === 0 ? -2 : 1)); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = maxSubarray(big); assert(typeof r === "number" && Date.now() - t0 < 200, "too slow, it must be one pass")

takeaway.key: At every item choose: extend the running subarray or restart here, cur = max(x, cur + x). Track the best cur. O(n) time, O(1) space.
mistakes: Starting best at 0, which breaks arrays where every number is negative.
Resetting cur to 0 instead of to x.
Forgetting that the subarray must be non-empty.

dryRun.title: Next greater item for [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]  (stack keeps indexes; shown as values)
dryRun.note: Items wait on the stack until something bigger arrives. Then they are popped and get their answer. Final answer: [4, 2, 4, -1, -1].

think.q:
const nums = [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]
const res = Array(nums.length).fill(-1)
const st = []
for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
  while (st.length && nums[st[st.length - 1]] < nums[i]) {
    res[st.pop()] = nums[i]
  }
  st.push(i)
}
console.log(res.join(","))
why: The 1 (index 1) is popped by the second 2, so its answer is 2. Both 2s are later popped by the 4, so each gets 4.
Items left on the stack at the end never found a bigger one, so they keep the starting -1.

think.q:
const t = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]
const ans = Array(t.length).fill(0)
const st = []
for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
  while (st.length && t[st[st.length - 1]] < t[i]) {
    const j = st.pop()
    ans[j] = i - j
  }
  st.push(i)
}
console.log(ans.join(","))
why: This is "daily temperatures": when index i pops index j, the wait is i - j days. Day 2 (75) waits 4 days for day 6 (76).
Because we need distances, the stack stores indexes, and the value is one lookup away.

think.q: There is a while loop inside a for loop. Why is the whole thing O(n) and not O(n²)?
opts: Because the while loop runs only once
Because every index is pushed once and popped at most once
It is O(n²) in the worst case
why: The total number of pops can never be more than the total number of pushes, which is n. So the inner loop does n steps in total, not n per item.
This "amortised" argument is why the pattern is worth knowing.

think.q: For "next greater item", how are the values on the stack ordered from bottom to top?
why: Anything smaller than the new item is popped before it is pushed, so what remains is a decreasing run. That is where the name "monotonic" comes from.
For "next smaller", flip the comparison and the stack becomes increasing.

think.q: Which question is a typical monotonic stack problem?
opts: Find two numbers that add to a target
For each day, how many days until a warmer day?
Count the paths in a grid
why: "Next greater / next smaller / how far until something bigger" is the signal.
It also appears in "largest rectangle in a histogram" and "trapping rain water".

try.task: Write nextGreater(nums). For each item, return the next bigger value to its right, or -1 if there is none. It must be O(n).
try.hint: Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is not known yet. For each i, while the item at the top is smaller than nums[i], pop it and set its answer. Then push i.

checks.t: empty array and one item, then a big input
checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(nextGreater([])) === "[]" && JSON.stringify(nextGreater([9])) === "[-1]", "edge cases"); const big = Array.from({ length: 100000 }, (_, i) => 100000 - i); const t0 = Date.now(); nextGreater(big); assert(Date.now() - t0 < 200, "too slow, it must be O(n)")

takeaway.key: Keep a stack of items still waiting for an answer. A new item pops everything smaller and becomes their answer. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
mistakes: Storing values when the answer needs a distance (store indexes).
Using <= when equal values should not count as "greater".
Forgetting that items left on the stack have no answer (use the default).
Calling the loop O(n²) or writing a nested scan instead.
